entities.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Great Pyramid of Giza, constructed around 2559 BCE, stands as the largest and oldest of the three pyramids in the Giza necropolis, located near Cairo, Egypt. This architectural marvel was commissioned by Pharaoh Khufu, also known as Cheops, and is a defining symbol of ancient Egyptian civilization, representing the apex of pyramid construction techniques. It holds immense significance as one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, drawing millions of visitors and scholars interested in its engineering and cultural implications.

The construction of the Great Pyramid involved an estimated 2.3 million limestone blocks, each weighing between 2.5 to 15 tons, quarried and transported from nearby sites. The pyramid originally stood at 146.6 meters (481 feet), though erosion has reduced its height over millennia. The project not only showcased the Egyptians’ advanced understanding of mathematics and astronomy but also demonstrated their ability to mobilize a large workforce, which included skilled laborers, architects, and slaves, particularly during the annual flooding of the Nile when agricultural work was paused.

The legacy of the Great Pyramid transcends its immediate geographical location, influencing subsequent architectural endeavors and cultural perceptions of power and immortality. The pyramid served as a model for later pharaohs, who adopted similar burial practices, thus shaping the funerary landscape of ancient Egypt and reinforcing the belief in the afterlife. It has also sparked numerous myths and theories regarding its construction methods and purpose, further embedding it in global historical discourse.
